chapter.name: Scope of Total Income & Residential Status

lectures.title: Residential Status of an Individual — Basic & Additional Conditions

cards.title: Why residential status? (Section 6)
cards.html:
Income tax
→
Person
→
Each year
→
Residential status
→
Days stayed in India
→
Tax
Residential Status
  • Individual
  • HUF
  • Company

Mr Rahul — Indian citizen (passport, UID) but stays in India only 10 days → the 10 days decide his status.

Every person's tax depends on their residential status, which is decided each tax year (e.g. 2026-27) from how many days the person stayed in India, not from citizenship. Passport, UID, voter ID, PAN or a bank account in India do not decide residence — only the days of stay.

Example: Mr Rahul is an Indian citizen (passport, UID) but stays in India only 10 days in the year → his status is decided by the 10 days.

Residential status is studied separately for Individual, HUF and Company.

cards.title: Basic conditions — Section 6(2)
cards.html:
Individual — Basic Conditions 6(2)any one satisfied → Resident
  • ① 182 daysstay in India during the tax year → Resident
  • ② 60 days + 365 days60 days in the tax year and 365 days in the last 4 years → Resident
Residential Status
  • Residentany 1 basic condition satisfied
  • Non-Residentno basic condition complete

An individual is Resident if he satisfies any one basic condition:

  1. Stays in India for 182 days or more during the tax year; or
  2. Stays in India for 60 days or more during the tax year and 365 days or more during the 4 preceding years.

If neither is satisfied → Non-Resident (NR).

cards.title: Exceptions — only basic condition 1 (182 days) applies
cards.html:
Exception — only rule 1 (182 days) applies
  • ① Indian originself, parent or grandparent · born in undivided India (before 1947)
  • ② Crew memberof an Indian ship
  • ③ Person going outside Indiafor employment
Indian origin — income from India more than 15 lakh
  • Basic condition 1182 days
  • Basic condition 2120 days (instead of 60) and 365 days in the last 4 years

For these individuals the 60-day rule (condition 2) is not available — only the 182-day test applies:

  1. An Indian citizen / person of Indian origin who comes on a visit to India. Indian origin = the person, either parent or any grandparent was born in undivided India (before 1947).
  2. An Indian citizen who leaves India for employment outside India.
  3. An Indian citizen leaving India as a crew member of an Indian ship.

Special case: if such a person of Indian origin has income from India of more than ₹15,00,000 and comes on a visit, condition 2 applies with 120 days instead of 60 days (120 days in the year and 365 days in the last 4 years).

cards.title: Counting days of stay
cards.html:
• Count day by day from 1 April to 31 March; the day of arrival and the day of departure are both counted as days in India.
  • India includes its territorial waters — up to 12 nautical miles from the coast.

cards.title: Additional conditions — Section 6(13)
cards.html:
Additional Conditions 6(13)checked only after the person is Resident
  • AC1resident in India 2 times in the last 10 years
  • AC2730 days in India in the last 7 years

Checked only after the individual is found Resident:

  1. Resident in India in at least 2 out of the 10 preceding tax years; and
  2. Stayed in India for 730 days or more during the 7 preceding tax years.

cards.q: Explain the basic and additional conditions for determining the residential status of an individual.
cards.a:
Basic conditions — Sec 6(2) (any one makes him Resident): (1) in India 182 days or more in the tax year; or (2) 60 days or more in the tax year and 365 days or more in the 4 preceding years. For an Indian citizen/person of Indian origin on a visit, an Indian citizen leaving for employment abroad, or a crew member of an Indian ship, only condition (1) applies; an Indian-origin visitor with Indian income above ₹15L gets condition (2) with 120 days instead of 60.

Additional conditions — Sec 6(13): (1) resident in at least 2 of the 10 preceding years; and (2) 730 days or more in India in the 7 preceding years.

ROR = 1 BC + both AC; RNOR = 1 BC + 0/1 AC; NR = no BC.

cards.title: Method for status questions
cards.html:
Count days in India this tax year
→
Check BC1, then BC2 (if allowed)
→
If resident: each of the last 10 years → AC1
→
Days in the last 7 years → AC2
→
Conclude ROR / RNOR / NR
  1. Count days in India in the current tax year (1 April – 31 March), month by month.
  2. Check BC1; if it fails and BC2 is allowed, add up days in the 4 preceding years.
  3. If Resident, list each of the 10 preceding years and decide whether he was resident in each (apply the BCs to that year) → AC1.
  4. Add days in the 7 preceding years → AC2.
  5. Conclude ROR / RNOR / NR.

lectures.title: Scope of Total Income by Residential Status & Tax Treatment of Gifts

cards.title: Status → which income is taxed
cards.html:
Person
→
Status
→
Income
→
Tax
Which income is taxed?
  • Source in India or received in IndiaROR ✓ · RNOR ✓ · NR ✓
  • Business outside India controlled from IndiaROR ✓ · RNOR ✓ · NR ✗
  • Accrues and received outside IndiaROR only

Person → status (basic + additional conditions) → which income is taxable → tax.

  • Income whose source is in India (accrues/arises in India, including within 12 nautical miles) or which is received in India is taxable for everyone — ROR, RNOR and NR.
  • Income that accrues and is received outside India is taxable only for ROR — except income from a business/profession controlled from India, which is also taxable for RNOR.

Examples: income from UP, salary received in India from USA, rent from Delhi → taxable for ROR, RNOR and NR. Business set up in India but controlled from abroad → all three. Business set up abroad but controlled from India → ROR and RNOR only.

cards.title: Received vs remitted — and foreign dividends
cards.html:
Dividend from foreign company
  • Received in IndiaMr Ram — Apple share dividend → ROR ✓ · NOR ✓ · NR ✓
  • Received outside IndiaMr John (USA) → ROR ✓ · NOR ✗ · NR ✗
  • Received in India: income first reaches the assessee in India (e.g. salary for a US job credited straight to a Citibank account in India) → taxable for all.
  • Remittance: income first received abroad and later sent to India → not 'received in India'; taxable only for ROR (because it was earned abroad).
  • Dividend from a foreign company: received in India (Mr Ram gets Apple dividend in India) → ROR, RNOR and NR; received outside India (Mr Johan gets it in USA) → ROR only.

cards.title: Tax treatment of gifts
cards.html:
Gifttransfer of property without consideration or for inadequate consideration
  • On marriagenot taxable
  • Relativenot taxable
  • Non-relative
    • Up to ₹50,000exempt
    • Exceeding ₹50,000fully taxable

Gift = transfer of movable or immovable property without consideration or for inadequate consideration.

  • On the occasion of marriage → not taxable (fully exempt).
  • From a relative → not taxable.
  • From a non-relative → exempt if the aggregate is up to ₹50,000; if it exceeds ₹50,000, the whole amount is taxable (e.g. ₹50,010 → fully taxable).

Relative includes: spouse; brother/sister; brother's/sister's spouse; brother's/sister's lineal ascendant; spouse's lineal ascendant; lineal ascendant; lineal descendant; any person for whom the individual is legal guardian.

cards.q: Classify as taxable or not: gift on marriage; gift from a brother of ₹2,00,000; gift from a friend of ₹50,010; gift from a friend of ₹40,000.
cards.a:
• Gift on the occasion of marriage — not taxable.
  • ₹2,00,000 from a brother (relative) — not taxable.

  • ₹40,000 from a friend (within ₹50,000) — exempt.

cards.q: Explain the scope of total income of an ROR, an RNOR and an NR.
cards.a:
• ROR — global income: income received/deemed received in India, income accruing/arising (or deemed to) in India, and income accruing and received outside India.
  • RNOR — income received in India + income accruing in India + income accruing outside India only if it is from a business controlled from, or a profession set up in, India.
  • NR — only income received/deemed received in India and income accruing/arising (or deemed to) in India.

Past untaxed income brought into India is not taxable for anyone.

lectures.title: Deemed Resident, Residential Status of HUF & Company

cards.title: Recap
cards.html:
Status
  • ROR1 BC + 2 AC
  • NOR1 BC + 0 AC = 1 BC + 1 AC
  • NR0 BC
ROR= 1 BC + 2 AC
RNOR = 1 BC + 0 ACor1 BC + 1 AC
NR= 0 BC

Exceptions (only the 182-day test): employee going outside India, crew member of an Indian ship, person of Indian origin on a visit. An Indian-origin visitor with Indian income above ₹15L → 182 days, or 120 days + 365 days in the last 4 years.

cards.title: Deemed Resident — IMPORTANT
cards.html:
Any personIndian citizen
→
Not paying tax in any country
→
Indian income more than 15L
→
Deemed resident
→
NOR

An Indian citizen whose total income from Indian sources exceeds ₹15 lakh and who is not liable to pay tax in any other country (by reason of domicile/residence) is deemed to be resident in India — and is treated as RNOR.

Example: Mr Ram in 2026: India 59 days (NR), UAE 180 days (not a tax resident), USA (not resident) — he pays tax nowhere. Indian income above ₹15L → deemed resident → RNOR.

cards.title: Residential status of a HUF
cards.html:
Residential Status (HUF)
  • ResidentIndia meetings / management decisions
    • Additional conditions (Karta)
      • 2 times residentlast 10 years
      • 730 dayslast 7 years
  • Non-Residentmeetings and management decisions not in India

ROR = BC + 2 AC · NOR = BC · NR = BC ✗

  • Resident — if the control and management of its affairs (meetings, management decisions) is wholly or partly in India.
  • Non-resident — if control and management is wholly outside India.

A resident HUF is ROR if its Karta satisfies both additional conditions (resident in 2 of the last 10 years and 730 days in the last 7 years); otherwise RNOR.

cards.title: Residential status of a company
cards.html:
Residential Status (Company)
  • Residentmeetings in India
  • Non-Residentmeetings not in India
  • Resident — an Indian company, or a company whose control and management (board meetings / place of effective management) is in India.
  • Non-resident — otherwise.

A company is only Resident or Non-resident — there is no ROR/RNOR split.

cards.q: During TY 2026-27, R and Sons HUF was partly controlled from India by its Karta R, an Indian citizen staying outside India who visits India regularly to manage the HUF. Determine the HUF's status if: (A) R has visited India 100 days every year for the last 12 years; (B) 110 days every year; (C) for the last 12 years — 50 days in each of the immediately preceding 4 years and 200 days each year before that.
cards.a:
Control and management is partly in India → the HUF is Resident. ROR or RNOR depends on the Karta's additional conditions.

(A) 100 days/yr: last 7 yrs = 700 < 730 AC2 ✗ → RNOR
(B) 110 days/yr: last 7 yrs = 770 ≥ 730;
resident in 2 of last 10 yrs ✓ → ROR
(C) last 7 yrs = 4 × 50 + 3 × 200 = 800 ≥ 730 ✓
years with 200 days → resident; 2 of 10 ✓ → ROR

cards.q: Who is a 'deemed resident'? What is his residential status?
cards.a: An Indian citizen whose total income, other than income from foreign sources, exceeds ₹15 lakh, and who is not liable to tax in any other country because of domicile or residence, is deemed to be resident in India. Such a deemed resident is always treated as Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR).

cards.q: How is the residential status of a HUF and of a company determined?
cards.a:
HUF: Resident if control and management of its affairs is wholly or partly in India; NR if wholly outside. A resident HUF is ROR if the Karta is resident in 2 of the 10 preceding years and has stayed 730+ days in India in the 7 preceding years; otherwise RNOR.

Company: Resident if it is an Indian company or its control and management (place of effective management) is in India; otherwise NR. There is no ROR/RNOR distinction for a company.
